oe.title: Hydrogels for absorbing lab spills
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Hydrogels have many polar –COOH groups that hydrogen bond strongly with water molecules: excellent for water and aqueous solutions of polar or ionic substances.
Non-polar liquids (e.g. hexane, oils) cannot hydrogen bond, so they will not be absorbed well.
The carboxyl groups are acidic: spilled alkalis (e.g. NaOH) would react (neutralisation) to form carboxylate salts. This could change the hydrogel, and heat may be released.
Spilled acids add H⁺, which suppresses ionisation of –COOH, so absorption may fall.
Ionic solutions: metal ions could be attracted to carboxylate groups, so absorption may change.
Safety: reactive spills (oxidising agents, concentrated acids) could react with the organic polymer.

oe.title: Cooking makes compounds water-soluble?
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Hydrolysis during cooking (heat, water, acid) can break large molecules into smaller, more polar ones.
Fats and oils (esters, non-polar, fat-soluble) hydrolyse to glycerol and fatty acids. Glycerol has three –OH groups and is water-soluble, so the statement can be true.

Proteins hydrolyse to amino acids, which have –NH₂ and –COOH groups and are more water-soluble. Cooking also denatures proteins (hydrogen bonds broken, shape changes), which can make them less soluble.
Esters (flavours) hydrolyse to carboxylic acids and alcohols. Short-chain products are water-soluble (hydrogen bonding with water).
But long-chain fatty acids are still mainly non-polar and not very water-soluble, and some cooking (e.g. frying) adds fat. So the statement is only partly accurate.

oe.title: Group 1 and Group 4 patterns
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Group 1 (alkali metals): all metallic bonding; low melting points that decrease down the group (weaker metallic bonds as atoms get bigger); all very reactive and form 1+ ions.
Group 4 changes down the group: C and Si are covalent networks (very high melting points), Ge is a metalloid, Sn and Pb are metallic. Bonding and structure change, so properties are less similar.
Covalent radius increases down both groups (extra shell and more shielding outweigh the extra nuclear charge).
First ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease down both groups. Group 1 values are low, so these elements lose electrons easily (strong reducing agents).
Chemical properties: Group 1 elements form ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl). Carbon and silicon form covalent compounds (CO₂ is molecular, SiO₂ a network); Sn and Pb can form ions.
Electrical conductivity: all Group 1 metals conduct; in Group 4, diamond and silicon conduct poorly, graphite and the metals Sn and Pb conduct.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Ionisation equation, e.g. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.
Sketch graph of melting point against atomic number for each group.
Diagrams of a covalent network (diamond) and a metallic lattice (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons).
Reaction with water, e.g. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

txt:
5.   Patterns in the Periodic Table

The Periodic Table is an arrangement of all the known elements in order of increasing atomic number. The reason why the elements are arranged as they are in the Periodic Table is to fit them all, with their widely diverse physical and chemical properties, into a logical pattern.

Periodicity is the name given to regularly-occurring similarities in physical and chemical properties of the elements.

Some Groups exhibit striking similarity between their elements, such as Group 1, and in other Groups the elements are less similar to each other, such as Group 4, but each Group has a common set of characteristics.

Adapted from Royal Society of Chemistry, Visual Elements (rsc.org)

oe.title: Seabirds and oil spills
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Crude oil is mainly non-polar hydrocarbons, insoluble in water (cannot hydrogen bond), so it floats and coats feathers.
Oil disrupts the structure that traps air, so feathers lose waterproofing and insulation (hypothermia) and buoyancy.
Vegetable oil is also non-polar, so it dissolves and loosens the crude oil (like dissolves like) without harming the bird. It is non-toxic if swallowed.
Washing-up liquid (detergent): the hydrophobic tail dissolves in the oil and the hydrophilic head dissolves in water, forming droplets (an emulsion) that rinse away.
Dilute detergent is used because concentrated detergent could strip natural oils from feathers or irritate skin.
Swallowed hydrocarbons are non-polar and can dissolve in fatty tissues, damaging organs.

oe.title: Investigating the viscosity of alcohols
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Factor 1, number of –OH groups: compare alcohols with similar chain length, e.g. propan-1-ol, propane-1,3-diol and propane-1,2,3-triol. More –OH groups give more hydrogen bonding, so higher viscosity.
Factor 2, chain length: compare methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol and pentan-1-ol. Longer chains have stronger London forces, so higher viscosity.

Factor 3, temperature: warm one alcohol using a kettle (water bath) and thermometer. Higher temperature means more kinetic energy, so intermolecular forces are overcome more easily and viscosity falls.
Method: time a ball bearing falling a fixed distance through each alcohol in a measuring cylinder or long glass tube (metre stick and timer). Or time a fixed volume draining from a burette or funnel.
Fair test: same volume, same temperature, same ball bearing and same distance; repeat and average.

Structures of propan-1-ol and propane-1,2,3-triol showing hydrogen bonds between molecules.

oe.title: Maximising profit, minimising environmental impact
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Choose reactions with high atom economy (fewer waste products) and high percentage yield.
Use catalysts: they lower activation energy, so lower temperatures (less energy cost) and faster rates. They can be reused.
For equilibrium reactions, choose temperature and pressure to favour products (Le Chatelier). Recycle unreacted reactants; remove products to shift the equilibrium.
Use excess of the cheaper reactant to make sure the expensive one is fully used.
Use energy efficiently: heat exchangers recover heat from exothermic reactions.
Choose cheap, available feedstocks; sell by-products; minimise waste and treat it before disposal; avoid toxic chemicals.
Consider safety, cost of raw materials, energy and plant; choose batch or continuous processes as appropriate.
Equations and calculations to consider
Atom economy = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100 (work through an example).
Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
Potential energy diagram showing Eₐ lowered by a catalyst; an equilibrium example such as N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.

oe.title: Determining the mass of oxalic acid in a rhubarb leaf
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Extract: crush or grind a weighed leaf, add water (oxalic acid is water-soluble) and filter. Make the filtrate up to a known volume in a volumetric flask.
Titration 1, acid–base: titrate pipetted samples against standard sodium hydroxide with an indicator. Oxalic acid is diprotic, so 2 mol NaOH react with 1 mol H₂C₂O₄.
Titration 2, redox: titrate against standard acidified potassium permanganate (self-indicating: purple to colourless, then permanent pink at the end-point). Warm the solution.
Repeat until concordant results (within 0·1 or 0·2 cm³) and use the average titre.
Calculate: moles = concentration × volume, use the mole ratio, then mass = moles × GFM (90 g mol⁻¹), and scale up for the total volume.
Limitations: other acids or reducing agents in the leaf (e.g. vitamin C) would also react.
Equations and calculations to consider
H₂C₂O₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O.
Redox: combine MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O with H₂C₂O₄ → 2CO₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (mole ratio 2 MnO₄⁻ : 5 H₂C₂O₄).

oe.title: Roles of chemicals in skin care products
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Water: polar solvent for ionic and polar ingredients (hydrogen bonding).
Fats and oils: non-polar, form a layer on the skin that stops water evaporating; more saturated fats are solid (thicker), oils are liquid (spread easily).
Emulsifiers (mono- and diglycerides): a hydrophilic –OH part dissolves in water and hydrophobic fatty acid tails in oil, so oil and water stay mixed.
Antioxidants (e.g. vitamin C, vitamin E): reducing agents that are oxidised in place of the product, preventing rancidity of oils. Free radical scavengers stop chain reactions from UV light.
Sun block: absorbs or reflects UV light, which can break bonds and form free radicals that damage skin.
Minerals (ionic compounds) dissolve in water.
Fragrances (esters, terpenes) are volatile, so they evaporate and give smell.

oe.title: Relationships between fats, oils, soaps, detergents and emulsifiers
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Fats and oils are esters (triglycerides) of glycerol and three fatty acids. Oils have more C=C (unsaturated, kinked chains, weaker London forces, liquid); fats are more saturated (solid).
Oils can be hardened into fats by hydrogenation (adding H₂ across C=C).
Soaps are made by alkaline hydrolysis of fats or oils with NaOH or KOH, giving glycerol and soap (salts of fatty acids).
Soaps and detergents clean the same way: hydrophobic tail in grease, hydrophilic head in water, forming ball-like structures that are washed away. Detergents (soapless) work in hard water.
Emulsifiers are made by reacting oils with glycerol to give mono- and diglycerides, which have free –OH (hydrophilic) and fatty acid chains (hydrophobic). They stop oil and water separating.

oe.title: Measuring and comparing the molar volume of gases
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Method 1, mass of a known volume: weigh an evacuated flask (vacuum pump), fill it with gas from a cylinder (N₂, H₂ or CO₂) and reweigh. Find the volume by filling with water and using a measuring cylinder. Moles = mass ÷ GFM; molar volume = volume ÷ moles.
Method 2, reaction producing a gas: react a weighed mass of magnesium (or zinc) with excess hydrochloric acid and collect the H₂ in a gas syringe or over water in an inverted measuring cylinder.
Or react a weighed mass of calcium carbonate or sodium carbonate with excess acid to make CO₂ (note CO₂ is slightly soluble in water, so a gas syringe is better).
Compare: repeat with different gases at the same temperature and pressure; the molar volumes should be about the same.
Accuracy: use excess acid, measure at room temperature and pressure, repeat and average.
Equations, calculations and diagrams to consider
Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
Molar volume = volume of gas ÷ number of moles (e.g. 0·024 g Mg = 0·001 mol gives about 24 cm³ H₂, so 24 l mol⁻¹).
Labelled diagram: flask with acid and metal connected by a delivery tube to a gas syringe.

oe.title: Melting points of non-metal elements
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Covalent network elements (carbon as diamond or graphite, silicon, boron): melting breaks strong covalent bonds, so very high melting points.
Covalent molecular elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, P₄, S₈, C₆₀): melting only breaks weak London dispersion forces between molecules, so low melting points.
Larger molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces: S₈ and P₄ are solids, Cl₂ is a gas; I₂ is a solid.
Monatomic noble gases have only weak London forces between atoms, so very low melting points that increase down the group (more electrons).
So the statement is true: structure (network, molecular or monatomic) and bonding (covalent bonds or intermolecular forces broken) determine melting point.
Diagrams to consider
Diagram of a covalent network (diamond) and a molecular element (e.g. P₄ or S₈) showing the forces broken on melting.
Sketch of melting points across period 3 (high for Si, low for P, S, Cl, Ar).
Diagram of temporary dipoles creating London forces.

oe.title: Collisions are the key to chemical reactions
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Collision theory: particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy, and with the correct orientation, to react.
Factors that increase collision frequency increase rate: concentration (or pressure for gases), surface area (smaller particles) and temperature.
Temperature mainly matters because more molecules have energy ≥ Eₐ, so more collisions are successful, not just more collisions.
Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower Eₐ, so more collisions are successful.
Activated complex: an unstable, high-energy arrangement formed at the top of the energy barrier.
Not every collision leads to reaction, so the statement is only partly true.

oe.title: The chemistry of cow's milk
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Milk is a mixture: water is a polar solvent for sugars (–OH groups hydrogen bond) and ions; fats and oils are non-polar and stay as droplets (an emulsion). Light scattering by the droplets makes it white.
Some molecules in milk (e.g. proteins) act as emulsifiers, keeping fat droplets dispersed: they have hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts.
Summer fats have higher melting points, so they are more saturated (fewer C=C). Straighter chains pack closer and give stronger London forces. Winter fats are more unsaturated.
Proteins are made of amino acids joined by peptide (amide) links. Heating or acid can denature them (hydrogen bonds broken), e.g. curdling.

Milk going off: oxidation of the sugars' hydroxyl groups gives acids, lowering the pH; this sours the milk and denatures proteins. Hydrolysis of fats gives free fatty acids (rancid smells), and unsaturated fats can be oxidised.
Antioxidants or refrigeration slow these reactions.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Diagram of an emulsion: fat droplet with emulsifier molecules (hydrophobic tails in, hydrophilic heads out).
Structure of a peptide link (–CONH–) and hydrogen bonding in a protein.
Oxidation of a primary alcohol group, –CH₂OH → –CHO → –COOH.
Hydrolysis of a fat to glycerol and fatty acids.

oe.title: Importance of electronegativity
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Bonding continuum: pure covalent (equal electronegativity, e.g. H₂, Cl₂), polar covalent (small difference, e.g. H–Cl gives δ+ and δ–), ionic (large difference, e.g. NaCl, usually metal and non-metal).
Trends: electronegativity increases across a period (more protons, similar shielding) and decreases down a group (more shells, more shielding).
Structure: ionic compounds form lattices with high melting points that conduct when molten or dissolved; covalent compounds are usually molecular (low melting points) or networks (e.g. SiO₂).
Polar bonds can give polar molecules if the shape is unsymmetrical (H₂O, NH₃), causing permanent dipole–permanent dipole interactions; symmetrical molecules (CO₂, CCl₄) are non-polar.
Hydrogen bonding when H is bonded to N, O or F (large difference) explains high boiling points (H₂O, HF) and solubility in water.
Properties: like dissolves like; polar or ionic substances dissolve in water, non-polar in non-polar solvents. Polar liquids are attracted to a charged rod.
Diagrams and data to consider

oe.title: Volumetric analysis procedures
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Standard solution: weigh solute accurately, dissolve in a beaker of deionised water, transfer with rinsings to a volumetric flask, make up to the mark (bottom of meniscus at eye level) and invert to mix.
Pipette: rinse with the solution to be measured, fill with a pipette filler to above the mark and adjust so the bottom of the meniscus is on the line; transfer to a conical flask.
Burette: rinse with the titrant, fill (remove the air bubble from the tip), and read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Add an indicator (or use a self-indicating reagent such as permanganate). Place a white tile under the flask, swirl, and add dropwise near the end-point.
Do a rough titration first, then repeat until concordant titres (within 0·1 or 0·2 cm³); average the concordant results.
Calculation: moles = c × V (in litres); use the mole ratio from the balanced equation; c = n ÷ V.
Equations, calculations and diagrams to consider
Example equation with mole ratio, e.g. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, or a redox example such as MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺ (1 : 5).
Worked example: concordant titre → moles of titrant → moles of analyte → concentration.
Labelled diagram of titration apparatus (burette, clamp, conical flask, white tile).

oe.title: Roles of compounds in dog food
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Fats and oils: energy source; more saturated fats are solid, giving texture. Unsaturated oils can become rancid (oxygen attacks C=C).
Antioxidants (e.g. vitamin C): reducing agents that are oxidised in place of the food. Free radical scavengers stop oxidation chain reactions, extending shelf life.
Emulsifiers (mono- and diglycerides): hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts keep oil and water mixed, so the food keeps its appearance and texture.
Proteins: hydrolysed in digestion to amino acids, which the dog uses to build its own proteins; essential amino acids must come from the diet.
Water: solvent, texture; but it allows hydrolysis (e.g. of fats to fatty acids, causing rancidity).
Flavour and aroma molecules (esters, aldehydes, terpenes): volatile, so they give smell; they can be lost on cooking or oxidised.
Fatty acids: may come from hydrolysis of fats; they are building blocks for fats.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Emulsifier at an oil–water interface.
Free radical chain reaction steps, and a scavenger forming a stable molecule.
Hydrolysis of a peptide link to amino acids; hydrolysis of a fat to glycerol and fatty acids.
Ion-electron equation for an antioxidant being oxidised, e.g. C₆H₈O₆ → C₆H₆O₆ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻.

oe.title: Distinguishing alcohols, aldehydes and ketones
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Use mild oxidising agents. Aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids; ketones are not oxidised; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised.
Fehling's solution (warm in a water bath): blue to brick-red precipitate with an aldehyde; no change with ketones and alcohols.
Tollens' reagent (warm in a water bath): silver mirror with an aldehyde; no change with ketones and alcohols.
Acidified potassium dichromate (warm): orange to green with aldehydes, primary and secondary alcohols; no change with ketones and tertiary alcohols.
Hot copper(II) oxide: black to brown (copper) with primary and secondary alcohols (forming aldehydes or ketones).
Combine tests: dichromate positive but Fehling's negative points to an alcohol (primary or secondary); both negative points to a ketone (or tertiary alcohol).
Safety: use a water bath, not a naked flame, as these compounds are flammable.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Ion-electron equations: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O; Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag; Cu²⁺ + e⁻ → Cu⁺.
Oxidation sequence: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol → ketone.
Results table and a labelled diagram of test tubes in a hot water bath.

oe.title: Maximising yields in reversible reactions
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations constant. Le Chatelier: a system shifts to oppose a change.
Concentration: add excess of a (cheaper) reactant, or remove product as it forms, to shift the equilibrium to the right.
Pressure (gases): high pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
Temperature: low temperature favours an exothermic forward reaction, high temperature an endothermic one. But low temperature is slow, so a compromise temperature is used.
Catalysts do not change the yield or position of equilibrium, but equilibrium is reached faster, so they save time and energy.
Recycling unreacted reactants increases the overall yield; balance yield against rate, cost and safety.
Equations, calculations and diagrams to consider
Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH negative; esterification as a reversible example.
Graph of yield against pressure at two temperatures.
Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

oe.title: The bonding continuum
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Position depends on the electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms. Zero difference gives pure covalent bonding (e.g. Cl₂, N–Br); a small difference gives polar covalent (e.g. H–Cl); a large difference gives ionic (e.g. NaF).
Electronegativity trends: increases across a period and decreases down a group, so metals with non-metals far apart in the table give ionic compounds.
Ionic compounds: lattices with high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved, often soluble in water.
Polar covalent molecules: permanent dipole–permanent dipole interactions (hydrogen bonding with N–H, O–H, F–H), higher boiling points, soluble in water.
Non-polar molecules: only London forces, low boiling points, insoluble in water, soluble in non-polar solvents.
Limitations: some compounds with intermediate differences show both ionic and covalent properties; shape matters (CO₂ has polar bonds but is non-polar).
Diagrams and data to consider
Diagram of the continuum (pure covalent → polar covalent → ionic) with examples and data booklet electronegativity values.
Dipole notation (δ+, δ–) on a polar bond; a lattice diagram for NaCl.
Shapes of CO₂ and H₂O to show symmetry.

oe.title: Mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate in a tablet
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Method 1, thermal decomposition: weigh the crushed tablet in a crucible, heat to constant mass and reweigh. Mass lost = H₂O + CO₂ (62 g per 2 mol NaHCO₃), then calculate the mass of NaHCO₃.
Method 2, gas volume: react a weighed tablet with excess acid and collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe. Moles CO₂ = volume ÷ molar volume = moles NaHCO₃.
Method 3, mass loss: react with excess acid in a flask on a balance (cotton wool plug) and record the mass of CO₂ lost.
Method 4, titration: dissolve the tablet, make up to a known volume, and titrate samples against standard HCl with an indicator. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (1 : 1).
Accuracy: repeat (concordant titres), use excess acid, assume other ingredients do not react.
Mass = moles × GFM (84 g mol⁻¹).
Equations, calculations and diagrams to consider
2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂; NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
Worked outline: e.g. 0·0120 mol CO₂ → 0·0120 mol NaHCO₃ → 0·0120 × 84 = 1·01 g.
Labelled diagrams: crucible heating to constant mass; gas syringe; titration set-up.

oe.title: Using position in the periodic table to predict properties
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Covalent radius: decreases across a period (more protons, same shell) and increases down a group (more shells, more shielding).
Ionisation energy: increases across a period and decreases down a group, as the outer electron is further away and more shielded.
Electronegativity follows the same trend as ionisation energy, so it predicts bond type: ionic between elements far apart, covalent between non-metals.
Melting points across a period: metallic (Na–Al) rise; covalent networks (B, C, Si) very high; covalent molecular (P₄, S₈, Cl₂) low; monatomic noble gases very low.
Chemical properties: low ionisation energy and electronegativity elements (left, bottom) are strong reducing agents; high electronegativity (top right, e.g. F₂, Cl₂) are strong oxidising agents.
Predict unknowns by trends, e.g. francium, astatine.
Equations, diagrams and data to consider
Equations for first and second ionisation, e.g. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻; Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g) + e⁻.
Sketch graphs of covalent radius and first ionisation energy against atomic number, using data booklet values.
Diagrams of a covalent network and a covalent molecular element.

oe.title: Chemicals in laundry products
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Soaps and detergents: the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail dissolves in grease and the hydrophilic (ionic) head in water. Agitation forms ball-like structures (micelles) that are washed away. Soapless detergents also work in hard water.
Bleaching agents are oxidising agents (e.g. hydrogen peroxide, chlorine-based bleach). They oxidise coloured compounds in stains to colourless ones.
Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins): proteases, lipases and amylases catalyse hydrolysis of proteins, fats and starch into smaller water-soluble molecules.
Enzymes work at lower temperatures (saves energy) but are denatured at high temperature (hydrogen bonds break and shape changes), so wash at the recommended temperature.
Water is a polar solvent for ionic and polar substances; non-polar stains need detergent.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Diagram of a detergent molecule and a micelle around a grease droplet.
Ion-electron equation for an oxidising agent, e.g. H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O.
Hydrolysis of a peptide link (protein stain) or an ester link (fat stain).
Sketch of enzyme activity against temperature (optimum, then denaturing).

oe.title: Bond polarity and the properties of molecular compounds
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Polar covalent bonds form between atoms with different electronegativities; the more electronegative atom carries δ−.
Whether a molecule is polar depends on its shape: symmetrical molecules (CO₂, CCl₄) are non-polar because the dipoles cancel.
Intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces in all molecules; permanent dipole–permanent dipole interactions in polar molecules; hydrogen bonding when H is bonded to N, O or F.
Hydrogen bonds are the strongest of these, so they raise melting and boiling points (e.g. water compared with H₂S; ethanol compared with propane).
Solubility: polar/hydrogen-bonded molecules dissolve in water ("like dissolves like"); non-polar molecules dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Viscosity: more hydrogen bonding (e.g. more –OH groups, glycerol) gives higher viscosity. Ice is less dense than water because of its open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
But the statement is not the whole story: London forces depend on molecule size, so a large non-polar molecule can have a higher boiling point than a small polar one.
Diagrams and data to consider
δ+/δ− labels on a polar bond, and a diagram of a symmetrical non-polar molecule.
Dotted hydrogen bond between two water or alcohol molecules.
Boiling point comparisons from the data booklet, e.g. alkanes vs alcohols of similar mass.

oe.title: Making cis-platin as profitably as possible
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
K₂PtCl₄ is by far the most expensive reactant, so it should be the limiting reactant, with the cheap reactants (KI, NH₃) in excess to make sure it is all converted.
The reaction is reversible: use excess of cheap reactants, or remove products (AgI is a precipitate, so it can be filtered off), to shift the equilibrium right.
The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature favours yield, but too low makes the rate slow: a compromise temperature. A catalyst speeds up the rate without changing the yield.
NH₃ is a gas: high pressure (or a sealed vessel) would keep it in solution and push the equilibrium right, but costs more.
Recover and recycle unreacted platinum compounds; silver could be recovered from AgI and reused (AgNO₃ is also costly).
Atom economy is low because of the many by-products (AgI, KNO₃, KCl): look for uses or sales of by-products.
Use the heat released by the exothermic reaction to reduce energy costs.
Calculations to consider
Mole ratios and masses to work out how much of each reactant is needed per gram of cis-platin.
Percentage yield and atom economy of the process.
